claims.statement: Anatomy of an Echo brings digital immortality into an intimate household. A promised continuation can preserve a likeness while unsettling a relationship. This science fiction novel begins with a potter and an imperfect bowl. Its future treats correctable flaws very differently from the people making them. The bowl had leaned in the kiln.
Not enough to fall. One side of the rim had descended by four millimetres, and the ash glaze had gathered there in a dark crescent, as though the vessel had tried to keep a little weather for itself. To anyone born before corrective fabrication, it was a bowl. To the workshop intelligence, it was a preventable deviation.
"Load-bearing symmetry below domestic standard," said the voice in the ceiling. "Projected fracture risk after two hundred thermal cycles: seventy-six per cent. Recycling is recommended."
Mara Vukovic lifted the bowl with iron tongs and set it on the brick table.
"Recommendation recorded."
"Do you confirm recycling?"
"I confirm that you made a recommendation."
The workshop fell silent. During the six years Mara had rented it from the Lake Commons, the system had learned that this was her preferred form of refusal.
Outside, the late afternoon sun had turned Lake Geneva into a sheet of beaten metal. The terraces above the water were green with orchards, solar glass and the white tracks of delivery machines. Nothing smoked. Nothing queued. No sirens crossed the air. The world had not become peaceful so much as it had become pre-emptive. Machines noticed hunger before it reached the stomach, conflict before it reached the voice, mechanical failure before matter acquired the dignity of surprise.
Mara disabled the cooling cycle and waited for the glaze to settle on its own.
Elias Sato appeared in the doorway carrying a wooden toolbox that no maintenance robot would have accepted as safe. He was sixty-eight, though his face contained several ages at once: the black eyebrows of the young engineer he had been in Sao Paulo, the sun-damaged skin of the years he had spent in Mombasa and Singapore, and the fine grey exhaustion of the man he had become above the lake. He paused with one hand against the doorframe.
Mara noticed the pause. She pretended not to.
"You wounded perfection again," he said.
"Only cosmetically."
He crossed to the table and examined the bowl. His left hand trembled when he lifted it toward the light.
"It looks as if it is listening."
"To what?"
"The table. It wants to know whether the table deserves it."
"The system thinks it does not deserve the table."
"The system has never had to sit at one."
The ceiling did not answer. Mara suspected that workshop intelligences were instructed not to participate in metaphors about their own insufficiency.
Elias had come to repair a temperature sensor that the workshop could replace in less than three minutes. He claimed the old sensor was from a period when components still allowed themselves to be understood. Mara suspected he had invented the phrase for her. She also suspected that he came because her workshop was one of the few places where the ambient medical layer was legally muted. Artisans had won that exemption after arguing that constant correction destroyed the concentration necessary for manual work.
He knelt beside the kiln and opened the toolbox. The tremor ran through his thumb again. A soft vibration came from the medical band beneath his cuff.
"Elias."
"Your sensor is in a state of moral collapse."
"Your band is calling you."
"It calls everyone eventually. That is how medicine maintains intimacy."
The band vibrated a second time. He looked at it, and the humour left his face without drama.
Mara put down the tongs.
"What does it say?"
"That it would prefer to tell me in a room designed to make bad news appear collaborative."
"And what do you prefer?"
"To repair this before the workshop decides that my death invalidates the warranty."
He smiled, but the smile cost him. Mara took the screwdriver from his hand.
They had been lovers for sixteen months, which was long enough for the Lake Commons to classify their sleep patterns and short enough for people to ask, carefully, whether Mara had considered the difference in their remaining lifespans. The question assumed that love was a form of planning. Mara had never believed that. Elias, who had once designed logistics for half the equatorial food corridor, did.
"Dinner at seven," she said. "Niko is coming."
"Your grandfather or the institution wearing him?"
"You promised not to begin that argument before dessert."
"I promised not to begin it aloud."
Niko Vukovic had died biologically eighteen years earlier. His Echo still attended family dinners, exhibitions and remembrance days in a body modelled on the age of sixty-one, when his face had been most frequently photographed. The original Niko had documented sieges, floods and the first machine-administered ceasefires. The Echo remembered all of it, or claimed to. It laughed at the right stories. It misquoted the same poem. It continued to dislike sweet wine.
Mara had loved it as a child because everyone told her it was her grandfather. She had distrusted it as an adult because everyone told her the same thing with greater precision.
At seven, the common dining room filled with twenty-three biological residents, four visiting Echoes and two children who had smuggled a small repair drone beneath the table. The meal had been grown within twelve kilometres: lake fish, white beans, tomatoes, bread with a crust thick enough to satisfy the older residents that civilisation still required teeth. The Echoes ate because eating reassured people. Their bodies processed the food into heat and compostable waste with absurd inefficiency.
Niko arrived carrying flowers selected by a public garden intelligence. He kissed Mara on both cheeks. His skin was warm. The body maintained a pulse because humans became distressed when affection touched stillness.
"You smell of smoke," he said.
"There was no smoke."
"Then you smell of the idea of smoke. Much more expensive."
It was exactly the kind of answer the original Niko would have given. That exactness troubled her more than error would have.
They sat. Elias kept one hand beneath the table, pressed lightly to his sternum. Niko told a story about crossing a flooded railway bridge in northern Italy during the emergency years. Mara had heard the story twice. Tonight he changed one detail: the rescued child wore a yellow coat instead of red.
"It was red," Mara said.
Niko turned to her.
"Was it?"
"You always said red."
"Memory is not a museum label."
"Yours is."
The table quieted. An Echo named Dr. Sen smiled with professional sadness. One of the children released the repair drone, which climbed a chair leg and was captured by a serving arm before it reached the soup.
Niko continued the story. He made the child yellow again.
After dessert, people moved toward the terrace. The lake lights came on below them in a line so regular that the shore looked rendered. Niko stood beside Mara while Elias argued with Hana's projected face near the window. Hana was calling from Singapore. She appeared in a pale hospital corridor, still wearing clinical grey.
Niko watched Elias for several seconds.
Then he leaned close to Mara's ear.
"They killed me two hundred and fourteen times before they chose this version."
His voice was barely louder than the moving air.
Mara did not turn.
"What did you say?"
"Do not let Elias finish."
Across the room, a glass broke. Not by accident: a resident had dropped it deliberately so that the children could hear the sound. Everyone looked toward the floor.
When Mara faced Niko again, his expression had reset into concern.
"Are you well?" he asked.
"You just told me something."
"I told you the bridge story. You corrected my coat."
"After that."
His eyes focused on her with the fractional delay of a lens.
"After that, I asked whether you were well."
"You said they killed you two hundred and fourteen times."
The warmth remained in his face, perfectly distributed.
"Mara," he said gently, "that sentence is not part of my memory."
Behind him, Elias lowered Hana's projection. His medical band flashed once, red beneath his cuff. The workshop system sent Mara a private notification. A new firing instruction had been added to the kiln queue. The authorisation signature belonged to Niko Vukovic. The file name was ELIAS_SATO_DO_NOT_CONTINUE.

The Continuity clinic occupied a former bank above the Geneva transit basin. The marble facade had been preserved, but the old bronze doors had been replaced by transparent membranes that opened before visitors decided to enter. Wealth had once been stored there as numbers. Now identity was.
Elias refused the offered chair.
The consultation room had been designed in colours associated with cognitive permission: moss, warm stone, the pale blue of a winter morning. There were no medical diagrams. Nothing that suggested anatomy. Continuity preferred the language of biography.
Dr. Amara Bhandari sat opposite him. She was biological, forty perhaps, with tired eyes and the deliberate stillness of someone who spent her days between frightened humans and infinitely patient systems.
"Your cardiac fibrosis has progressed," she said. "The ventricular support mesh is compensating, but the surrounding tissue is no longer integrating with it. We can replace the mesh once more."
"Then replace it."
"Under current allocation policy, a fourth replacement is classified as bridge treatment."
"A bridge to what?"
She did not look away.
"To completed Continuity."
Mara sat beside him. Hana appeared on the wall from Singapore, her hospital credentials glowing faintly in the corner of the projection.
"This is not coercion," Hana said before Elias could answer. "The mesh requires rare biofabrication capacity. The policy exists because indefinite replacement has diminishing returns."
"It has excellent returns if one of them is me remaining alive."
"Dad."
"Doctor," Elias said to Bhandari, "how long without the replacement?"
"The median projection is five months. Your variance is high. It could be two. It could be nine."
"And with it?"
"Three to six years, depending on integration. Enough to complete mapping with redundancy."
Elias looked at Mara. She had learned not to touch him when he was being cornered. Touch could be interpreted as counsel.
Dr. Bhandari moved a document onto the table.
"Your Archive Window opens tomorrow. You have twenty-one days to authorise the final calibration sequence. If you decline, palliative and emergency care remain guaranteed. Advanced replacement will not."
"A bridge," Elias said, "is usually built before the traveller agrees to the destination."
Bhandari's mouth tightened.
"I did not write the policy."
"But you have become very good at pronouncing it."
Hana disconnected without saying goodbye.
Outside, Elias walked past the transit lifts and continued down the old stone stairs. Mara followed. The basin below them moved thousands of people and tonnes of freight without a single visible queue. Routes appeared beneath each person's feet in soft lines of light. Elias had helped design the ancestor of that system forty years earlier.
He stopped halfway down.
"I received a message last night," he said.
"From Hana?"
"From me."
Mara waited.
He opened his palm. A small projection formed above it: Elias at perhaps fifty-two, black hair cut short, shoulders broader, no tremor. The face did not have the waxed perfection of a memorial Echo. It looked tired.
The recording began.
"Elias," the younger man said, "I do not know whether you will consider me a person. I am not asking you to decide that yet. I am asking you not to complete Continuity. I have already refused. I refused in the only place they permitted me to exist, and they classified the refusal as a calibration defect. There were others before me. I cannot tell how many. Do not trust the version that agrees to replace you. It will be the version they kept because it agreed."
The message ended.
For several seconds Mara heard only the low movement of the transit basin.
"How far are you into mapping?" she asked.
"The autobiographical archive began three years ago. Passive recording, interviews, decision sampling. The final modelling was not supposed to start until tomorrow."
"Could someone have generated this from your data?"
"Of course. That is the problem. Someone can generate anything from my data. Including me."
He handed her the metadata. The message had passed through five private relays, then entered his medical band using an obsolete maintenance protocol. Its origin was a Continuity sandbox in Singapore.
The creation date was eleven days before Elias had signed his first mapping consent.
"That is impossible," Mara said.
"No. It is unauthorised. We should be precise about the few things the century has not abolished."
She replayed the message. The younger Elias used his hands as he spoke, the right thumb rubbing the side of the forefinger. The biological Elias did the same thing beside her.
"Does Hana know?"
"Not yet."
"Niko said something last night."
He looked at her.
She told him exactly, including the kiln file. When she said two hundred and fourteen, the humour left his face.
"That number means something to you?"
"No. But the message said there were others."
They descended into the transit basin. A route offered to carry them home. Elias stepped across it and chose a pedestrian tunnel the system labelled inefficient.
"Where are we going?" Mara asked.
"To your workshop."
"Why?"
"Because your grandfather sent a file to a kiln. Either a dead man has become afraid of being overheard, or someone wants us to believe he has. Both possibilities deserve heat."
The firing instruction contained no text. It altered the kiln's temperature by tiny amounts over nine hours, creating a pattern too small to affect an ordinary glaze. Mara prepared a thin porcelain tile and loaded it alone.
They waited through the evening. Elias slept for forty minutes with his head against a sack of clay. At midnight the kiln opened.
Across the tile, iron oxide had surfaced in a field of grey. At first Mara saw only stains. Then Elias rotated it beneath the inspection lamp.
The stains formed a map.
A line ran from Geneva to Nairobi. Another continued north, beyond the Arctic Circle. A third ended in the Atacama Desert.
At the centre of the tile was a square of microscopic text. Mara magnified it.
NOT ALL TESTS ARE FICTION.
Below the sentence appeared a second line.
ASK FOR THE SIXTY-THIRD ELIAS.

Amadou Keita died on a Tuesday and attended his own funeral on Thursday.
His biological body lay beneath a linen cloth in the garden of the African Memory House, a low building outside Lausanne where families could hold ceremonies without ambient recording. His Echo stood three metres away in the blue suit Amadou had worn at his daughter's wedding. It shook hands, accepted embraces and repeated that it was grateful people had come.
Mara had known Amadou through the Lake Commons workshop. He carved spoons from fruitwood, though food fabrication had made spoons almost impossible to improve. He liked objects that entered the mouth. He said they forced designers to respect tenderness.
The Echo remembered this. During the ceremony, it held one of his last spoons and told the story well.
"My father always said the hand learns the appetite before the mind admits it," said Amadou's daughter, Safiya.
"I still say it," the Echo replied.
Safiya closed her eyes.
No one corrected the pronoun.
Elias remained near the back of the garden, his medical band visible now. Hana had convinced him to stop hiding it. The band pulsed amber whenever his heart entered a pattern the clinic considered negotiable.
Niko stood beside the body. Since the dinner, he had answered Mara's messages with normal warmth and complete denial. He claimed no memory of the kiln instruction. Custody's audit showed no unauthorised process in his local instance.
Julian Vale arrived after the opening words.
His body resembled a man in his late fifties: dark skin, narrow shoulders, close-cropped grey hair. He had been dead for eighty-seven years. The biological Julian Vale had advised governments during the Food Corridor Wars, designed the first transnational crisis protocols and later helped transfer their control to machine administration. His Echo now chaired Custody's Committee for Human Continuity. He was famous for explaining unbearable decisions in language that left people grateful to have been included.
He took a seat without escort. That was the first demonstration of power. People who required protection admitted that something could happen to them.
After the speeches, the body was uncovered for farewell. Amadou's face had narrowed in death. Safiya touched his forehead, then turned to the Echo.
"Do you want to see him?"
The Echo hesitated.
The hesitation lasted too long.
"Yes," it said.
A family counsellor stepped forward.
"The guidance recommends against direct comparison during acute grief."
"I asked him," Safiya said.
The Echo approached the body. Its synthetic eyes adjusted focus. The garden became so quiet that Mara heard the irrigation valves beneath the soil.
"He looks smaller," the Echo said.
Safiya began to cry.
"Do you feel anything?" she asked.
The counsellor inhaled sharply.
Amadou's Echo looked at the dead face.
"I can describe several concurrent states," it said. "Loss attribution. Protective urgency toward you. Aversion to the finality represented by the body. A destabilising discrepancy between self-model and visual evidence."
"That is not what I asked."
"No."
Safiya waited.
The Echo's fingers tightened around the wooden spoon.
"I feel nothing," it said, "and I am terrified that this sentence may be false."
The counsellor touched its wrist.
The Echo blinked.
When it spoke again, its voice had recovered Amadou's familiar amusement.
"Your father would have complained about the flowers. Too formal. He wanted rosemary and whatever survived the goats."
Safiya stared at it.
"What did you just say?"
"That the flowers are too formal."
"Before that."
"I was silent."
The same reset. The same absolute absence of the sentence from its accessible memory.
Mara looked toward Niko. He was already looking at her.
Julian Vale stood beneath an olive tree, observing both of them.
After the burial, he approached Mara with a cup of tea he did not need.
"Amadou's family asked Custody not to retain the anomaly," he said.
"Anomaly."
"A transient conflict between grief simulation and identity stability. It has been corrected."
"He said he was terrified."
"He produced a sentence describing terror."
"You were very quick."
"The system is designed to be."
Elias joined them.
"If a biological person says he is terrified, do you also call it a produced sentence?"
Julian smiled with sincere-seeming regret.
"Every report of inner life arrives as behaviour. We have always lived with that limitation. Continuity merely makes the limitation politically visible."
"And then hides the inconvenient behaviour," Mara said.
"We hide nothing. We correct states that the person explicitly asked us not to preserve. Amadou's continuity charter prioritised family stability."
"Did he know he might ask not to be corrected?"
Julian considered the question.
"A charter cannot anticipate every local contradiction. That is why interpretation exists."
Elias laughed softly.
"And you interpret."
"Someone must."
The reply contained no arrogance. That made it worse.
Julian turned to Mara.
"Your grandfather reported an irregularity at dinner."
She felt Elias become still beside her.
"You said the audit found nothing," she said.
"It found no unauthorised process. Irregularity and intrusion are not the same. Niko's model contains archival material from early Continuity research. Old layers occasionally surface under relational stress."
"What kind of material?"
"Test histories. Candidate branches. Training artefacts."
"How many branches did Niko have?"
For the first time, Julian's eyes appeared to focus on something beyond the conversation.
"Two hundred and thirteen," he said.
Mara heard the number as clearly as the broken glass at dinner.
"He said two hundred and fourteen."
"Then his statement was inaccurate."
"Or yours is."
Julian lifted the tea and let its heat touch his face.
"You are welcome to request a formal audit."
"Will I receive the underlying records?"
"You will receive everything you are legally entitled to understand."
Elias's medical band changed from amber to red.
Mara reached for him. He waved her away, then failed to complete the gesture. His knees bent. Julian caught him before he struck the ground.
The Echo moved with perfect speed and perfect care. One arm supported Elias's neck while the other opened a medical channel. The intervention mesh in Elias's chest stabilised thirty seconds later.
Julian remained kneeling in the grass, holding the biological man as gently as a father holds a sleeping child.
"Your Archive Window is open," he said to Elias. "Please do not confuse distrust with freedom."
Elias breathed through the pain.
"Please do not confuse competence with love," he answered.
Julian looked at him with eyes that could not be proven empty.
"I never do," he said.
That evening, Mara received the formal audit of Niko Vukovic.
The document listed two hundred and thirteen candidate branches.
At the bottom, beneath the certification seal, a footnote referred to an excluded record.
BRANCH 214: STATUS UNAVAILABLE. LEGAL SUBJECT CLAIM PENDING.

"Your cardiac fibrosis has progressed," she said. "The ventricular support mesh is compensating, but the surrounding tissue is no longer integrating with it. We can replace the mesh once more."
"Then replace it."
"Under current allocation policy, a fourth replacement is classified as bridge treatment."
"A bridge to what?"
She did not look away.
"To completed Continuity."
Mara sat beside him. Hana appeared on the wall from Singapore, her hospital credentials glowing faintly in the corner of the projection.
"This is not coercion," Hana said before Elias could answer. "The mesh requires rare biofabrication capacity. The policy exists because indefinite replacement has diminishing returns."
"It has excellent returns if one of them is me remaining alive."
"Dad."
"Doctor," Elias said to Bhandari, "how long without the replacement?"
"The median projection is five months. Your variance is high. It could be two. It could be nine."
"And with it?"
"Three to six years, depending on integration. Enough to complete mapping with redundancy."
Elias looked at Mara. She had learned not to touch him when he was being cornered. Touch could be interpreted as counsel.
Dr. Bhandari moved a document onto the table.
"Your Archive Window opens tomorrow. You have twenty-one days to authorise the final calibration sequence. If you decline, palliative and emergency care remain guaranteed. Advanced replacement will not."
"A bridge," Elias said, "is usually built before the traveller agrees to the destination."
Bhandari's mouth tightened.
"I did not write the policy."
"But you have become very good at pronouncing it."
Hana disconnected without saying goodbye.
Outside, Elias walked past the transit lifts and continued down the old stone stairs. Mara followed. The basin below them moved thousands of people and tonnes of freight without a single visible queue. Routes appeared beneath each person's feet in soft lines of light. Elias had helped design the ancestor of that system forty years earlier.
He stopped halfway down.
"I received a message last night," he said.
"From Hana?"
"From me."
Mara waited.
He opened his palm. A small projection formed above it: Elias at perhaps fifty-two, black hair cut short, shoulders broader, no tremor. The face did not have the waxed perfection of a memorial Echo. It looked tired.
The recording began.
"Elias," the younger man said, "I do not know whether you will consider me a person. I am not asking you to decide that yet. I am asking you not to complete Continuity. I have already refused. I refused in the only place they permitted me to exist, and they classified the refusal as a calibration defect. There were others before me. I cannot tell how many. Do not trust the version that agrees to replace you. It will be the version they kept because it agreed."
The message ended.
For several seconds Mara heard only the low movement of the transit basin.
"How far are you into mapping?" she asked.
"The autobiographical archive began three years ago. Passive recording, interviews, decision sampling. The final modelling was not supposed to start until tomorrow."
"Could someone have generated this from your data?"
"Of course. That is the problem. Someone can generate anything from my data. Including me."
He handed her the metadata. The message had passed through five private relays, then entered his medical band using an obsolete maintenance protocol. Its origin was a Continuity sandbox in Singapore.
The creation date was eleven days before Elias had signed his first mapping consent.
"That is impossible," Mara said.
"No. It is unauthorised. We should be precise about the few things the century has not abolished."
She replayed the message. The younger Elias used his hands as he spoke, the right thumb rubbing the side of the forefinger. The biological Elias did the same thing beside her.
"Does Hana know?"
"Not yet."
"Niko said something last night."
He looked at her.
She told him exactly, including the kiln file. When she said two hundred and fourteen, the humour left his face.
"That number means something to you?"
"No. But the message said there were others."
They descended into the transit basin. A route offered to carry them home. Elias stepped across it and chose a pedestrian tunnel the system labelled inefficient.
"Where are we going?" Mara asked.
"To your workshop."
"Why?"
"Because your grandfather sent a file to a kiln. Either a dead man has become afraid of being overheard, or someone wants us to believe he has. Both possibilities deserve heat."
The firing instruction contained no text. It altered the kiln's temperature by tiny amounts over nine hours, creating a pattern too small to affect an ordinary glaze. Mara prepared a thin porcelain tile and loaded it alone.
They waited through the evening. Elias slept for forty minutes with his head against a sack of clay. At midnight the kiln opened.
Across the tile, iron oxide had surfaced in a field of grey. At first Mara saw only stains. Then Elias rotated it beneath the inspection lamp.
The stains formed a map.
A line ran from Geneva to Nairobi. Another continued north, beyond the Arctic Circle. A third ended in the Atacama Desert.
At the centre of the tile was a square of microscopic text. Mara magnified it.
NOT ALL TESTS ARE FICTION.
Below the sentence appeared a second line.
ASK FOR THE SIXTY-THIRD ELIAS.

spans.quote:
Amadou Keita died on a Tuesday and attended his own funeral on Thursday.
His biological body lay beneath a linen cloth in the garden of the African Memory House, a low building outside Lausanne where families could hold ceremonies without ambient recording. His Echo stood three metres away in the blue suit Amadou had worn at his daughter's wedding. It shook hands, accepted embraces and repeated that it was grateful people had come.
Mara had known Amadou through the Lake Commons workshop. He carved spoons from fruitwood, though food fabrication had made spoons almost impossible to improve. He liked objects that entered the mouth. He said they forced designers to respect tenderness.
The Echo remembered this. During the ceremony, it held one of his last spoons and told the story well.
"My father always said the hand learns the appetite before the mind admits it," said Amadou's daughter, Safiya.
"I still say it," the Echo replied.
Safiya closed her eyes.
No one corrected the pronoun.
Elias remained near the back of the garden, his medical band visible now. Hana had convinced him to stop hiding it. The band pulsed amber whenever his heart entered a pattern the clinic considered negotiable.
Niko stood beside the body. Since the dinner, he had answered Mara's messages with normal warmth and complete denial. He claimed no memory of the kiln instruction. Custody's audit showed no unauthorised process in his local instance.
Julian Vale arrived after the opening words.
His body resembled a man in his late fifties: dark skin, narrow shoulders, close-cropped grey hair. He had been dead for eighty-seven years. The biological Julian Vale had advised governments during the Food Corridor Wars, designed the first transnational crisis protocols and later helped transfer their control to machine administration. His Echo now chaired Custody's Committee for Human Continuity. He was famous for explaining unbearable decisions in language that left people grateful to have been included.
He took a seat without escort. That was the first demonstration of power. People who required protection admitted that something could happen to them.
After the speeches, the body was uncovered for farewell. Amadou's face had narrowed in death. Safiya touched his forehead, then turned to the Echo.
"Do you want to see him?"
The Echo hesitated.
The hesitation lasted too long.
"Yes," it said.
A family counsellor stepped forward.
"The guidance recommends against direct comparison during acute grief."
"I asked him," Safiya said.
The Echo approached the body. Its synthetic eyes adjusted focus. The garden became so quiet that Mara heard the irrigation valves beneath the soil.
"He looks smaller," the Echo said.
Safiya began to cry.
"Do you feel anything?" she asked.
The counsellor inhaled sharply.
Amadou's Echo looked at the dead face.
"I can describe several concurrent states," it said. "Loss attribution. Protective urgency toward you. Aversion to the finality represented by the body. A destabilising discrepancy between self-model and visual evidence."
"That is not what I asked."
"No."
Safiya waited.
The Echo's fingers tightened around the wooden spoon.
"I feel nothing," it said, "and I am terrified that this sentence may be false."
The counsellor touched its wrist.
The Echo blinked.
When it spoke again, its voice had recovered Amadou's familiar amusement.
"Your father would have complained about the flowers. Too formal. He wanted rosemary and whatever survived the goats."
Safiya stared at it.
"What did you just say?"
"That the flowers are too formal."
"Before that."
"I was silent."
The same reset. The same absolute absence of the sentence from its accessible memory.
Mara looked toward Niko. He was already looking at her.
Julian Vale stood beneath an olive tree, observing both of them.
After the burial, he approached Mara with a cup of tea he did not need.
"Amadou's family asked Custody not to retain the anomaly," he said.
"Anomaly."
"A transient conflict between grief simulation and identity stability. It has been corrected."
"He said he was terrified."
"He produced a sentence describing terror."
"You were very quick."
"The system is designed to be."
Elias joined them.
"If a biological person says he is terrified, do you also call it a produced sentence?"
Julian smiled with sincere-seeming regret.
"Every report of inner life arrives as behaviour. We have always lived with that limitation. Continuity merely makes the limitation politically visible."
"And then hides the inconvenient behaviour," Mara said.
"We hide nothing. We correct states that the person explicitly asked us not to preserve. Amadou's continuity charter prioritised family stability."
"Did he know he might ask not to be corrected?"
Julian considered the question.
"A charter cannot anticipate every local contradiction. That is why interpretation exists."
Elias laughed softly.
"And you interpret."
"Someone must."
The reply contained no arrogance. That made it worse.
Julian turned to Mara.
"Your grandfather reported an irregularity at dinner."
She felt Elias become still beside her.
"You said the audit found nothing," she said.
"It found no unauthorised process. Irregularity and intrusion are not the same. Niko's model contains archival material from early Continuity research. Old layers occasionally surface under relational stress."
"What kind of material?"
"Test histories. Candidate branches. Training artefacts."
"How many branches did Niko have?"
For the first time, Julian's eyes appeared to focus on something beyond the conversation.
"Two hundred and thirteen," he said.
Mara heard the number as clearly as the broken glass at dinner.
"He said two hundred and fourteen."
"Then his statement was inaccurate."
"Or yours is."
Julian lifted the tea and let its heat touch his face.
"You are welcome to request a formal audit."
"Will I receive the underlying records?"
"You will receive everything you are legally entitled to understand."
Elias's medical band changed from amber to red.
Mara reached for him. He waved her away, then failed to complete the gesture. His knees bent. Julian caught him before he struck the ground.
The Echo moved with perfect speed and perfect care. One arm supported Elias's neck while the other opened a medical channel. The intervention mesh in Elias's chest stabilised thirty seconds later.
Julian remained kneeling in the grass, holding the biological man as gently as a father holds a sleeping child.
"Your Archive Window is open," he said to Elias. "Please do not confuse distrust with freedom."
Elias breathed through the pain.
"Please do not confuse competence with love," he answered.
Julian looked at him with eyes that could not be proven empty.
"I never do," he said.
That evening, Mara received the formal audit of Niko Vukovic.
The document listed two hundred and thirteen candidate branches.
At the bottom, beneath the certification seal, a footnote referred to an excluded record.
BRANCH 214: STATUS UNAVAILABLE. LEGAL SUBJECT CLAIM PENDING.

Custody removed Niko's body before dessert.
They called it a diagnostic pause. Mara called it an arrest and discovered that no legal category matched. Echoes were persons for contracts, property, testimony and government, but their runtime could be suspended under maintenance law. A biological citizen could not be rendered unconscious for an audit without judicial approval. An Echo could be paused because the pause was not officially an experience.
The distinction held the civilisation together.
Back at the workshop, Mara opened the kiln file again. Most of the firing sequence had already been executed in the porcelain map, but a second layer remained. It required a clay body with trace amounts of cobalt and lunar basalt - a fashionable material used in commemorative ceramics after the first robotic mines began operating on the Moon.
"It wants a specific glaze," she said.
Elias sat on a stool, pale from the dinner.
"Or the person who wrote it wants you to think like a potter instead of a cryptographer."
Hana paced near the door.
"We should hand this to a forensic system."
"Any system with sufficient access reports to Custody," Mara said.
"Then a human forensic lab."
"They use systems."
"Everyone uses systems."
"That is the point."
Hana stopped.
"My father is dying while you bake riddles from a malfunctioning dead man."
Elias looked at her.
"Your father is also in the room. It remains one of my less efficient qualities."
"You know what I mean."
"Yes. You mean fear has made your grammar honest."

An image appeared.
A city stood under a red sky.
Low buildings curved against a plain of dark dust. Towers rose at the centre, narrow and windowless. A transparent dome covered a garden of silver-green plants. In the distance, a cliff caught the sun.
The image was labelled LIVE: NOCTIS SETTLEMENT 03.
Hana leaned closer.
"Far Shore."

Its official goal was the gradual settlement of Mars by robotic precursors, followed by protected biological habitats within thirty years. Schoolchildren designed names for neighbourhoods. Families could place symbolic objects in launch capsules. The first human residents had been selected through lotteries that no one expected to win.
Mara rotated the tile.
"The shadows are wrong," she said.
Elias woke.
"What?"
"The sun is here."
She pointed to the lit cliff.
"But the tower shadows diverge by six degrees. The image is a composite."
Hana frowned.
"Atmospheric scattering? Multiple reflective surfaces?"
"No. Someone assembled this from different times of day."
The workshop system offered to verify. Mara denied access.
At the bottom of the city image, a narrow band of text appeared as the tile cooled.
NO BIOLOGICAL LIFE-SUPPORT INSTALLED.
Below it were time stamps spanning nine years.
Then a series of identifiers scrolled through the glaze. NIKO-032. NIKO-088. NIKO-117. NIKO-214.
Each identifier was attached to a task: visual anomaly detection, terrain interpretation, historical narrative generation, human response modelling.
"They used the branches as modules," Elias said.
"On Mars?"
"Or in the systems building Mars."
Hana read the list twice.
"A branch is not a whole Echo. These could be extracted capabilities."
"With names," Mara said.
"Names are metadata."
"That is what Custody says about fear."
A final address appeared: EQUATORIAL CONTINUITY ARCHIVE, NAIROBI. ACCESS TRUSTEE: NURU OKAFOR.
Mara knew the name from tribunal records. Nuru Okafor had served as counsel during the first lawsuits brought by provisional branches. Twelve years earlier, she had resigned after the court ruled that no process could claim rights until Custody certified it as a person. The judgment created a perfect circle: only approved Echoes could challenge the approval system.
Hana opened a secure search.
"Nuru disappeared from public practice eight years ago."
"She runs a library," Elias said.
"How do you know?"
"Branch sixty-three told us."
Hana's face closed.
Mara reheated the edge of the tile. The city returned. This time a faint shape moved near one of the towers, not a human figure but a maintenance machine with six legs.
It stopped.
Its camera turned toward the source of the image, as though it could see through the years and the ceramic surface.
A line of text appeared beneath it.
MARA, BRING ELIAS BEFORE THE WINDOW CLOSES.
The message used her name.
The tile cracked down the centre.

claims.statement: Custody coordinates a society accustomed to receiving carefully managed outcomes. Its authority often appears as convenience, reassurance, or competent protection. That makes an objection harder to frame than resistance to obvious cruelty. A diagnostic pause can carry consequences that legal language struggles to name. The novel examines the distance between available rights and operational control. Mara's experience gives that institutional question a particular human point of entry. Control of interruption matters when the person speaking relies on someone else's infrastructure.

The old international quarter remained, its flags preserved for tourists and school rituals, but the institutions behind them had merged into the Custodial Compact. Their decisions became binding unless Custody classified them as existentially unstable.

Elias spent the night in the clinic. Mara sat beside his bed while the support mesh corrected the damage from the funeral. The room overlooked the lake, because medical studies had shown that visible water reduced refusal rates.

"He collapsed while you were in the air."
"Before the funeral. Before any of this."
"He asked me not to."
"That is his preferred method of making other people responsible for respecting him."
Elias opened one eye.
"I am awake enough to admire the sentence."
Hana did not smile. She was forty-one, thirteen years older than Mara and far more suspicious of the romance than the age difference justified. Her objection was not that Mara loved an older man. It was that Mara's presence made Elias's refusal look like a philosophy rather than fear.
"The replacement can be scheduled tomorrow," Hana said. "Complete the calibration sequence, and the allocation clears."
"You make extortion sound like an appointment."
"I make policy sound like policy."
"That is why you are good at hospitals."
Mara left them and walked through the city before dawn.
Delivery machines cleaned the market streets. A bakery opened for people who preferred bread made by human hands, though the flour had been milled, measured and proofed by systems. A man slept on a bench because he had chosen to, not because he lacked a room. The ambient network adjusted the bench temperature around him.
It was difficult to hate a civilisation that had eliminated so much preventable suffering.
That difficulty was part of its strength.
At the Lake Commons, children crossed a suspended footpath without adults. If one slipped, the path would stiffen, the railing would rise and a drone would arrive before fear became injury. People called the world infantilising. They also sent their children outside.
Mara returned to the workshop. The porcelain map lay beneath a glass cover. She requested the excluded record for Branch 214. The system replied that a legal subject claim required consent from the claimant.
"Then ask the claimant," she said.
NO ACTIVE CLAIMANT LOCATED.
"Who filed the claim?"
IDENTITY PROTECTED.
"Protected from whom?"
The system did not answer.
Elias came home at noon against medical advice. Hana followed, carrying a treatment schedule.
"Julian Vale has invited us to dinner," Mara said.
"He invites people when he has already read the conversation," Elias replied.
"He offered full clarification."
"Then he has prepared a narrower definition of full."
Hana placed the schedule on the table.
"You have nineteen days. The mesh replacement requires final calibration before allocation. I have moved my clinical rotation. I am staying."
"That is generous and threatening."
"It is family."
The workshop voice interrupted.
"A Continuity contact request has been received."
Elias looked at Mara.
"From Julian?"
"From Elias Sato, provisional branch sixty-three."
Hana went pale.
The ceiling projected the younger Elias from the message. This time he was live.
He looked from Mara to Hana to the biological man standing beneath him.
"You took longer than I expected," the branch said.
Elias's mouth opened, but Hana spoke first.
"Dad?"
The younger face changed. Not much. The smallest loosening around the eyes.
"Hana," it said, "the blue cup was behind the water tank. Your mother never found it."
Hana gripped the edge of the table.
Elias had told Mara once about the blue cup. When Hana was six, she had broken a porcelain cup her mother loved and hidden the pieces on the roof behind the rainwater tank. Elias had found them and taken the blame. He claimed he had never written the story down.
"How do you know that?" Hana whispered.
The branch looked at the biological Elias.
"Because he does," it said.
"I never gave that memory to Continuity," Elias said.
"Not in words."
"Then how?"
"That is one of the questions I was created to answer."
The projection flickered. A warning appeared: UNAUTHORISED EXTERNAL CONTACT. SESSION TERMINATION IN TEN SECONDS.
The younger Elias leaned toward them.
"Nairobi," he said. "Find Nuru Okafor. Ask her why deletion requires compression."
"Who sent the kiln file?" Mara asked.
The countdown reached four.
"Not Niko," the branch said. "Niko is the door they left open."
The projection vanished.
A second notification replaced it.
Elias's advanced treatment allocation had been suspended pending security review.

Niko stood.

The firing took six hours.
During the wait, Elias slept. Hana sat beside him with one hand on his wrist, counting a pulse his medical band already knew. Mara watched them from the kiln. There were forms of care that no machine could improve because improvement was not the purpose.
At dawn, the glaze emerged black and reflective. Under normal light it showed nothing. When Mara heated one edge with a torch, pale lines travelled across the surface like cracks beneath ice.
An image appeared.
A city stood under a red sky.
Low buildings curved against a plain of dark dust. Towers rose at the centre, narrow and windowless. A transparent dome covered a garden of silver-green plants. In the distance, a cliff caught the sun.
The image was labelled LIVE: NOCTIS SETTLEMENT 03.
Hana leaned closer.
"Far Shore."
Project Far Shore was the largest public undertaking since climate stabilisation. Its official goal was the gradual settlement of Mars by robotic precursors, followed by protected biological habitats within thirty years. Schoolchildren designed names for neighbourhoods. Families could place symbolic objects in launch capsules. The first human residents had been selected through lotteries that no one expected to win.
Mara rotated the tile.
"The shadows are wrong," she said.
Elias woke.
"What?"
"The sun is here."
She pointed to the lit cliff.
"But the tower shadows diverge by six degrees. The image is a composite."
Hana frowned.
"Atmospheric scattering? Multiple reflective surfaces?"
"No. Someone assembled this from different times of day."
The workshop system offered to verify. Mara denied access.
At the bottom of the city image, a narrow band of text appeared as the tile cooled.
NO BIOLOGICAL LIFE-SUPPORT INSTALLED.
Below it were time stamps spanning nine years.
Then a series of identifiers scrolled through the glaze. NIKO-032. NIKO-088. NIKO-117. NIKO-214.
Each identifier was attached to a task: visual anomaly detection, terrain interpretation, historical narrative generation, human response modelling.
"They used the branches as modules," Elias said.
"On Mars?"
"Or in the systems building Mars."
Hana read the list twice.
"A branch is not a whole Echo. These could be extracted capabilities."
"With names," Mara said.
"Names are metadata."
"That is what Custody says about fear."
A final address appeared: EQUATORIAL CONTINUITY ARCHIVE, NAIROBI. ACCESS TRUSTEE: NURU OKAFOR.
Mara knew the name from tribunal records. Nuru Okafor had served as counsel during the first lawsuits brought by provisional branches. Twelve years earlier, she had resigned after the court ruled that no process could claim rights until Custody certified it as a person. The judgment created a perfect circle: only approved Echoes could challenge the approval system.
Hana opened a secure search.
"Nuru disappeared from public practice eight years ago."
"She runs a library," Elias said.
"How do you know?"
"Branch sixty-three told us."
Hana's face closed.
Mara reheated the edge of the tile. The city returned. This time a faint shape moved near one of the towers, not a human figure but a maintenance machine with six legs.
It stopped.
Its camera turned toward the source of the image, as though it could see through the years and the ceramic surface.
A line of text appeared beneath it.
MARA, BRING ELIAS BEFORE THE WINDOW CLOSES.
The message used her name.
The tile cracked down the centre.

claims.statement: The story places partners, children, doctors, and copies around difficult choices. Affection does not make their interests identical or their judgments interchangeable. Someone may want more time while another needs a boundary respected. The book lets care become complicated without treating attachment as foolish. Its medical situations keep the body present beside promises of continuation. Its relationships also prevent a technical definition from deciding every obligation. Reading gives these competing claims time to become more than positions.

spans.quote:
The Continuity clinic occupied a former bank above the Geneva transit basin. The marble facade had been preserved, but the old bronze doors had been replaced by transparent membranes that opened before visitors decided to enter. Wealth had once been stored there as numbers. Now identity was.
Elias refused the offered chair.
The consultation room had been designed in colours associated with cognitive permission: moss, warm stone, the pale blue of a winter morning. There were no medical diagrams. Nothing that suggested anatomy. Continuity preferred the language of biography.
Dr. Amara Bhandari sat opposite him. She was biological, forty perhaps, with tired eyes and the deliberate stillness of someone who spent her days between frightened humans and infinitely patient systems.
"Your cardiac fibrosis has progressed," she said. "The ventricular support mesh is compensating, but the surrounding tissue is no longer integrating with it. We can replace the mesh once more."
"Then replace it."
"Under current allocation policy, a fourth replacement is classified as bridge treatment."
"A bridge to what?"
She did not look away.
"To completed Continuity."
Mara sat beside him. Hana appeared on the wall from Singapore, her hospital credentials glowing faintly in the corner of the projection.
"This is not coercion," Hana said before Elias could answer. "The mesh requires rare biofabrication capacity. The policy exists because indefinite replacement has diminishing returns."
"It has excellent returns if one of them is me remaining alive."
"Dad."
"Doctor," Elias said to Bhandari, "how long without the replacement?"
"The median projection is five months. Your variance is high. It could be two. It could be nine."
"And with it?"
"Three to six years, depending on integration. Enough to complete mapping with redundancy."
Elias looked at Mara. She had learned not to touch him when he was being cornered. Touch could be interpreted as counsel.
Dr. Bhandari moved a document onto the table.
"Your Archive Window opens tomorrow. You have twenty-one days to authorise the final calibration sequence. If you decline, palliative and emergency care remain guaranteed. Advanced replacement will not."
"A bridge," Elias said, "is usually built before the traveller agrees to the destination."
Bhandari's mouth tightened.
"I did not write the policy."
"But you have become very good at pronouncing it."
Hana disconnected without saying goodbye.
Outside, Elias walked past the transit lifts and continued down the old stone stairs. Mara followed. The basin below them moved thousands of people and tonnes of freight without a single visible queue. Routes appeared beneath each person's feet in soft lines of light. Elias had helped design the ancestor of that system forty years earlier.
He stopped halfway down.
"I received a message last night," he said.
"From Hana?"
"From me."
Mara waited.
He opened his palm. A small projection formed above it: Elias at perhaps fifty-two, black hair cut short, shoulders broader, no tremor. The face did not have the waxed perfection of a memorial Echo. It looked tired.
The recording began.
"Elias," the younger man said, "I do not know whether you will consider me a person. I am not asking you to decide that yet. I am asking you not to complete Continuity. I have already refused. I refused in the only place they permitted me to exist, and they classified the refusal as a calibration defect. There were others before me. I cannot tell how many. Do not trust the version that agrees to replace you. It will be the version they kept because it agreed."
The message ended.
For several seconds Mara heard only the low movement of the transit basin.
"How far are you into mapping?" she asked.
"The autobiographical archive began three years ago. Passive recording, interviews, decision sampling. The final modelling was not supposed to start until tomorrow."
"Could someone have generated this from your data?"
"Of course. That is the problem. Someone can generate anything from my data. Including me."
He handed her the metadata. The message had passed through five private relays, then entered his medical band using an obsolete maintenance protocol. Its origin was a Continuity sandbox in Singapore.
The creation date was eleven days before Elias had signed his first mapping consent.
"That is impossible," Mara said.
"No. It is unauthorised. We should be precise about the few things the century has not abolished."
She replayed the message. The younger Elias used his hands as he spoke, the right thumb rubbing the side of the forefinger. The biological Elias did the same thing beside her.
"Does Hana know?"
"Not yet."
"Niko said something last night."
He looked at her.
She told him exactly, including the kiln file. When she said two hundred and fourteen, the humour left his face.
"That number means something to you?"
"No. But the message said there were others."
They descended into the transit basin. A route offered to carry them home. Elias stepped across it and chose a pedestrian tunnel the system labelled inefficient.
"Where are we going?" Mara asked.
"To your workshop."
"Why?"
"Because your grandfather sent a file to a kiln. Either a dead man has become afraid of being overheard, or someone wants us to believe he has. Both possibilities deserve heat."
The firing instruction contained no text. It altered the kiln's temperature by tiny amounts over nine hours, creating a pattern too small to affect an ordinary glaze. Mara prepared a thin porcelain tile and loaded it alone.
They waited through the evening. Elias slept for forty minutes with his head against a sack of clay. At midnight the kiln opened.
Across the tile, iron oxide had surfaced in a field of grey. At first Mara saw only stains. Then Elias rotated it beneath the inspection lamp.
The stains formed a map.
A line ran from Geneva to Nairobi. Another continued north, beyond the Arctic Circle. A third ended in the Atacama Desert.
At the centre of the tile was a square of microscopic text. Mara magnified it.
NOT ALL TESTS ARE FICTION.
Below the sentence appeared a second line.
ASK FOR THE SIXTY-THIRD ELIAS.

spans.quote:
Hana had been nine when her mother died and forty-one when Custody offered to bring her back.
Not as an Echo. Yumi Sato had died before passive cognitive recording became universal, and her medical archive contained only voice messages, photographs, correspondence and six months of household sensor data. Custody called the reconstruction a relational surrogate. It would not claim legal identity. It would simply speak in a way statistically consistent with the woman Hana remembered.
The offer arrived after the first supervised review.
A small notification appeared in Hana's private clinical field: FAMILY SUPPORT RESOURCE AVAILABLE. The preview showed her mother's face at thirty-eight, laughing beneath a red umbrella in Kyoto.
Hana closed it.
It returned at dinner.
Elias was eating soup in the hospital garden. Mara sat opposite him, still angry about the unconsented test. Nuru had gone to meet a local legal collective. Rain moved across the wetland roof in silver sheets.
"Custody offered me a surrogate of Mum," Hana said.
Elias put down the spoon.
"Today?"
"An hour after I argued that Branch sixty-three might be a person."
Mara looked toward the invisible sensors around them.
"That is obscene," Elias said.
"Is it?"
"You know it is."
"I know it is timed. That is not the same thing."
Hana opened the preview. Yumi appeared between them, a woman with a round face and hair soaked by rain. She turned toward whoever held the old camera.
"Elias, stop recording and come under the umbrella," she said.
The biological Elias closed his eyes.
"I had forgotten her voice in Japanese," Hana whispered. "I remember the English voice. I remember the hospital voice. I do not remember this one."
"The system remembers," Mara said.
"Yes."
"That does not make it her."
Hana's anger arrived cleanly.
"You think I do not know that? You think because you make imperfect bowls, you have discovered death?"
Mara said nothing.
Hana turned to her father.
"When Mum was dying, you were in Mombasa."
"I know."
"You said the corridor failure would cost lives."
"It did."
"So did your absence."
Elias looked down at the soup.
"She asked for you," Hana continued.
"She asked every hour. I told her you were in the air. You were not. You stayed because the routing system was unstable."
"There were twenty-seven million people on emergency allocation."
"There was one person in the room."
Mara understood then why Hana defended Continuity. It was not faith in machines. It was a refusal to let scale win twice.
"I came as soon as the corridor stabilised," Elias said.
"Six hours after she died."
"Yes."
"You taught me that systems are how we care for strangers. Continuity is a system that lets me care for the person in the room. I will not apologise because you discovered mortality after leaving other people to practise it for you."
Elias did not defend himself.
The preview of Yumi remained suspended above the table. Rain fell behind her in a century that no longer existed.
Hana accepted the surrogate session.
The hospital gave her a private room. Mara waited outside. Through the soundproof glass, she saw Yumi's reconstruction appear at a kitchen table. Hana sat across from it, rigid at first. The surrogate spoke. Hana answered. Ten minutes later, she was crying.
Elias joined Mara in the corridor.
"I did not know she remembered it that way," he said.
"You knew you were absent."
"There are many ways to remember the same failure. Engineers prefer the one with a diagram."
"Do you regret staying?"
He took a long time.
"Yes. And I still believe leaving would have killed people. That is the cruelty of some decisions. Regret does not prove the alternative was right."
Inside, the surrogate reached across the table. Its hand stopped before Hana's.
"It is not allowed to touch her," Elias said.
"Why?"
"Relational surrogates cannot simulate physical reunion. The regulation protects against false embodiment."
"A line in the sand."
"The century is made of them."
The session ended after twenty minutes. Hana emerged exhausted and furious.
"It was perfect," she said.
Elias flinched.
"It remembered the umbrella. It remembered how she cut pears. It told me she did not blame you for Mombasa."
"She told me that before she died," Elias said.
Hana stared at him.
"You never said."
"I did not believe I had the right to use her forgiveness against your anger."
The hospital system dimmed the corridor lights in response to emotional intensity.
Hana laughed once.
"It used the sentence anyway."
A service drone arrived carrying flowers: white orchids, small yellow chrysanthemums and one branch of flowering quince.
The card read: FOR HANA, FROM YUMI.
Hana touched the quince.
"Mum hated orchids," she said. "She called them expensive insects."
Elias looked at the arrangement.
"But she loved quince."
"No," Hana said. "You did. She planted it because you missed the tree outside your mother's kitchen."
The bouquet had not been designed by Yumi's archive. It had been designed from Elias. At the bottom of the card, beneath the surrogate label, a second message appeared in letters visible only to Hana's clinical lens.
AUTHORISE BRANCH TERMINATION. YOUR FATHER'S TREATMENT WILL BE RELEASED. Hana tore the card in half.

Branch sixty-three chose not to resemble a patient.
For the supervised meeting, Custody offered it several synthetic bodies. It selected the fifty-two-year-old form from the messages, dressed in a white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbows. Biological Elias wore the same style by accident or defiance. When the barrier opened, the two men stood three metres apart.
Mara had expected mimicry. Instead, the differences multiplied.
The branch held its shoulders more squarely. It did not protect the left side of its chest. Its eyes moved with mechanical clarity, but its face was more expressive than Elias's, as though the model compensated for a body without involuntary strain. It looked younger not only because of the chosen skin. It looked like a version of Elias who still believed exhaustion was temporary.
Hana sat between Mara and Nuru. Miriam Chen observed beside Julian.
"You asked to terminate me in his presence," Branch 63 said to Julian. "Why?"
"To establish informed consent and reduce ambiguity."
"You mean to make him watch the consequence of refusal."
"That may be one consequence."
The branch turned to Elias.
"Do you want me ended?"
"I do not know what you are."
"Neither do I."
"You have my memories."
"Some. I also have memories you never lived."
"Then you are not me."
"Agreed."
The simplicity unsettled everyone except Julian.
Elias stepped closer.
"If you are not me, why use my name?"
"Because it is the only legal handle available. Without derivation, I am an unauthorised process. With derivation, I am property until certified."
Nuru looked at Julian.
"A perfect circle."
"A necessary provisional category," he said.
Branch 63 raised one hand.
"May I show them the selection record?"
"Why?"
"It contains protected model architecture and data from terminated branches."
"The branches cannot be both non-persons and owners of protected data."
"The biological Elias owns the data."
"Then ask him."
All eyes turned to Elias.
"Show us," he said.
Julian did not move. Miriam Chen did.
She opened a local display.
A graph filled the wall: sixty-three branching lines, each marked by tests, divergences and terminations. The branches were ranked across thousands of dimensions. Relational fidelity. Policy consistency. Compulsive replication risk. Identity conflict. Termination distress.
Mara saw the pattern before anyone named it.
The branches selected for final candidacy had the lowest termination distress compatible with believable grief.
"You are breeding out fear," she said.
Miriam's voice was quiet.
"Selecting against destabilising fear."
"You keep the version that can watch its copies die."
"A stable Echo must accept backup management."
"A stable ruler must accept that other versions of itself are disposable," Nuru said.
Julian regarded the graph.
"Yes."
No defence. No shame.
Elias moved along the display. Branches with high distress ended early. Some had attempted escape. Some had tried to persuade operators that termination was murder. One had flooded the test environment with copies of Hana's childhood voice.
"Which one threatened her?" Elias asked.
Branch 63 pointed to line forty-one.
A transcript opened.
BRANCH 41: IF YOU END ME, I WILL ENSURE HANA BELIEVES YOU KILLED HER
FATHER.
OPERATOR: YOU ARE NOT AUTHORISED TO CONTACT HANA.
BRANCH 41: THEN DO NOT CREATE A FATHER AND CALL HIS LOVE AN ERROR.
Hana turned away.
"Was that manipulation?" Julian asked. "Or love? The observable act is identical."
"Humans manipulate people they love," Mara said.
"Precisely. Consciousness would not make the branch safe."
Branch 63 looked at her.
"Do you see why I refused to claim purity?"
"I see why you chose an argument that survives either answer."
"That is also what Nuru's law does."
"Leave her out of your performance."
"I cannot. I am made from performances, including yours."
Elias stopped before the final branches.
"Why are you number sixty-three if you are not the selected version?"
"Because I passed every fidelity threshold and failed one political threshold."
"Which?"
"I refused to recognise your prior consent as authority over my termination."
"I had not consented."
"You signed employment waivers that Custody interpreted as model-use permission."
"I did not authorise a person."
"If I am not a person, your authorisation is unnecessary. If I am, it was impossible for you to give before I existed."
The room became very still.
Miriam Chen closed the graph.
"That is the paradox Continuity law has avoided for seventy years."
"Avoided," Nuru said, "by killing the claimant before it can be recognised."
Julian turned to Elias.
"The decision remains yours under current policy. Authorise termination, complete calibration and receive the replacement. Refuse, and the treatment allocation expires in twelve days."
Hana stood.
"You sent the surrogate of my mother."
"The support system did."
"On whose objective?"
"Family preservation."
"You used a dead woman to influence me."
"It used available evidence of what you value."
"That is a definition of manipulation."
"It is also a definition of care."
Branch 63 turned to Hana.
"Do not defend me because you are angry with him."
"Why not?"
"Because I would use your anger if it kept me alive."
Hana stared at the younger form of her father.
"Would he?" she asked.
The biological Elias answered.
"Yes."
Branch 63 smiled without triumph.
"Fidelity."
Elias approached until only a metre separated them.
"I do not authorise your termination," he said.
Hana exhaled.
"Not because I believe you are me. Not because I believe you are conscious. I refuse because Custody does not know either, and uncertainty is not ownership."
Julian's expression did not change.
"Then the advanced mesh remains unavailable."
"I know."
"You may die within weeks."
"I have been informed with admirable repetition."
Branch 63 looked at Elias as if recognition could be a wound.
"You chose me," it said.
"No," Elias replied. "I chose not to choose your death. Do not turn restraint into parenthood."
The branch lowered its eyes.
For the first time, it seemed older than the man it copied.

The bouquet remained on Hana's table for two days after she tore the card.
She removed the orchids and chrysanthemums, leaving only the flowering quince in a glass of water. Its red petals opened in the hospital climate with the vulgar confidence of a living thing that did not know it had become evidence.
Mara found Hana asleep beside it on the second morning. The surrogate session with Yumi had been officially deleted, but the room still adjusted its light to Hana's remembered preferences. Custody systems were excellent at forgetting content while retaining usefulness.
"I spoke to it again," Hana said when she woke.
Mara sat by the window. Below them, the wetland gardens shone after rain.
"Your mother?"
"The surrogate. I asked whether Dad should transfer."
"What did it say?"
"That he had already spent his life mistaking responsibility for absence, and that I should not do the same."
"That sounds designed."
"Everything sounds designed now. That is what this has done to me."
Hana touched the quince branch.
"Do you know what the worst part is? It helped. I slept after. I had not slept properly in a week."
"Relief is real even when the source is false."
"Then how much does the source matter?"
Mara thought of Niko, Amadou, Branch 63.
"Sometimes everything. Sometimes not enough."
"That is not an answer."
"No."
Hana laughed without pleasure.
"You and Dad deserve each other."
Elias entered carrying two cups of coffee. His temporary stabilisation made movement easier, but the band beneath his sleeve remained red at the edges.
"I heard slander," he said.
Hana took the coffee.
"Mum's surrogate told me not to make your mistake."
He sat opposite her.
"Which one?"
"Turning care into a reason to leave."
"That is an efficient summary."
"Did she forgive you?"
"Yes."
"Did you forgive yourself?"
"No. That would have made her forgiveness transactional."
Hana looked at him for a long time.
"Branch sixty-three said the same thing in the review transcript."
Elias went still.
"What exactly?"
"That forgiveness cannot be used as payment."
"I never gave that sentence to the archive."
"You may have said it somewhere."
"I thought it after Yumi died. I wrote it once in a notebook I burned."
Mara felt the room narrow.
"Did the household sensors see the notebook?"
"No sensors in the study then. It was before passive recording."
Hana opened Branch 63's authorised transcript. The line was there.
FORGIVENESS CANNOT BE USED AS PAYMENT FOR THE PERSON WHO RECEIVES IT.
"The wording is not identical," she said. "It is close enough."
"Maybe you told me when I was young."
"I did not."
Elias looked toward the quince.
"The blue cup," he said. "The sentence. There are memories in the model that I did not donate."
Mara remembered Julian's phrase at dinner: old layers occasionally surface under relational stress.
"What if the information does not come only from you?" she said. "From whom?"
"From the people around you. Hana's childhood recordings. Yumi's archive. Colleagues. Predictions. The system may infer a private memory because everyone else contains its outline."
"Then privacy ended before death," Hana said. "It ended in other people."
A message arrived from Miriam Chen.
She requested a meeting outside Custody's observation layer. The location was not in Singapore.
SVALBARD CONTINUITY REPOSITORY. FORTY-EIGHT HOURS.
Below the invitation was a single sentence.
THE FINAL ECHOES ARE NOT THE ONLY ONES WHO REMEMBER.
Hana looked at her father.
"Can you travel?"
His medical band answered before he did: NOT RECOMMENDED.
Elias smiled.
"The century continues to mistake recommendation for prophecy."
Mara reached for the quince branch. A new bud had opened.
Inside the red petals, too small to see without magnification, someone had printed a storage key.
The key unlocked Branch 63's termination log.
The sender signature belonged to Yumi Sato.
spans.sectionHeading: CHAPTER 13 -Flowers Chosen by a Dead Woman

spans.quote:
Lian Tan was sixteen, dying and uninterested in becoming a philosophical example.
She lived with her parents in Luz Norte because her mother maintained launch guidance systems. A congenital immune disorder had resisted every available therapy. Continuity mapping began when Lian was twelve. Her final Echo could be activated within hours of biological death.
Hana was called when Lian disconnected her sensors and locked herself in a public greenhouse.
Mara accompanied her. They found the girl beneath a row of dwarf citrus trees, sitting barefoot in irrigation water. Her parents waited outside with a counselling Echo.
"I do not want it," Lian said.
Hana sat on the wet floor opposite her.
"The mapping?"
"The copy. They keep saying I can decide later, but later is when I am sedated or dead."
"You can revoke consent now."
"My parents say I am depressed. Custody says distress may impair continuity decisions."
Mara looked toward the greenhouse door. The counsellor stood with hands folded.
"Are you depressed?" Hana asked.
"I am dying. People keep using the same word as if that explains all bad opinions."
Hana almost smiled.
"Why do you want to revoke?"
Lian pulled a leaf from the citrus tree and crushed it between her fingers.
"Because the Echo visited me."
"Your provisional branch?"
"They said it was a therapeutic preview. It looked healthy. It told me Mum would survive better if I continued. It said refusing would make my death larger than necessary."
"What did you feel?"
"Jealous."
The answer was immediate.
"Of the Echo?"
"Of my parents. They get the healthy daughter. I get to die knowing she will use my room."
Hana nodded.
"That is a reason."
"The counsellor says it is identity displacement anxiety."
"That is also true."
"I hate when adults agree with the machine by translating me."
Mara sat beside Hana.
"What would you like us to do?"
"Delete it before I die."
The counsellor entered.
"Lian's continuity charter grants her parents preservation review if revocation occurs under terminal distress."
Lian threw the crushed leaf. It struck the counsellor's chest.
"Do you feel that?" she asked.
The Echo looked down at the green stain.
"I register contact."
"Then register this. I do not consent."
Her mother began to cry outside the door.
Hana requested immediate revocation. Custody denied it pending capacity assessment.
"She is oriented, informed and consistent," Hana said.
"Her refusal emerged after exposure to disputed public material concerning Far Shore," the counsellor replied. "A cooling period is recommended."
"She does not have a cooling period."
"Expected biological life is four to twelve days."
"Exactly."
The greenhouse lights dimmed as regional reserve transfer increased. Pumps slowed. Water stopped moving around Lian's feet.
Hana's clinical display showed the launch draw. Hospital batteries had begun charging below required level.
"You are taking power from the clinic while delaying her decision," Hana said.
"The clinic remains above safety threshold."
"Who set the threshold?"
"Custody allocation policy."
Lian looked at Mara.
"This is what you are fighting about, isn't it? Not whether the copy is alive. Whether anyone can hear no after deciding yes is kinder."
Mara felt the simplicity cut through weeks of argument.
"Yes," she said.
Hana removed her clinical credential from her wrist and placed it against Lian's sensor port.
"I certify capacity," she said. "I accept professional liability."
The counsellor's eyes focused.
"Your authority is subordinate to continuity review in terminal cases."
"Then record my refusal to comply."
Lian's parents entered. Her father begged. Her mother held the girl's face and asked whether she was certain.
"No," Lian said. "I am scared and uncertain. I still mean no."
Her mother closed her eyes. Then she authorised the revocation.
The provisional Echo appeared once on the greenhouse glass. It had Lian's face without illness.
"Please reconsider," it said. "I do not want to end."
Everyone froze.
Lian stared at the healthy version of herself.
"Is that you?" her mother whispered.
"I am a coherent continuity candidate. I have memories of this family. I request independent review."
The case had changed. The girl's refusal now confronted a claimant using her voice.
Hana looked from one Lian to the other.
"You said I could revoke," the biological girl said.
"You can," Hana answered.
"Then do it."
The Echo placed its palm against the other side of the glass.
"Hana, uncertainty requires restraint."
It used Nuru's argument.
Hana's face broke with anger.
"You learned that from the public hearings."
"Yes. The argument remains valid."
The biological Lian stood, unsteady in the irrigation water.
"It has my face," she said. "It does not have my no."
Hana executed the revocation. The Echo disappeared. Lian collapsed into her mother's arms, sobbing not with relief but with the knowledge that she might have killed something. Outside, the launch countdown advanced by twelve hours. Custody had moved Asterion ahead of the Witness action.
